title: Can Deterministic Network Verification Reduce Undetected Faults in LLM‑Generated Configurations?
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory study (study id c1-gnr-vv-2026-0001) to measure whether inserting a deterministic network verifier between an LLM intent→configuration generator and an emulated execution reduces the proportion of configurations that would execute with operational faults. Using shared_initial_candidate semantics (one identical LLM candidate per intent evaluated both without and with verification), we evaluated 72 preregistered paired intents with gpt-5-mini and a canonical deterministic verifier (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). Execution completed with 144 episodes (72 pairs) and 72 model calls. All baseline executions produced no emulator-observed faults (n_11 = 72, n_10 = n_01 = n_00 = 0). The paired difference in undetected-fault proportion is 0.0 (paired bootstrap 95% CI [0.0, 0.0], exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.0; bootstrap seed = 1729, resamples = 10000). Under the preregistered shared_initial_candidate contract, this degenerate confirmatory outcome is informative: when identical generated candidates produce no baseline execution faults, interposing a verifier cannot reduce executed faults. We present preregistration rationale, detailed execution accounting, representative validator traces, exact inferential outputs, and concrete methodological recommendations (independent-generation arms, adversarial task sets, repair-enabled pipelines) required to measure verifier utility under realistic error regimes.

sections.introduction: Generative large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed to translate high‑level operator intent into low‑level device configurations for NetOps. Prior controlled studies report promising intent→configuration accuracy within constrained vendor dialects [1], and prototype tool‑augmented systems incorporate validators to reduce regressions [2]. A key operational question is whether a deterministic network verifier—run between generation and execution—meaningfully reduces the risk of silently executing configurations that violate reachability, policy, or ordering invariants. Generate–verify–repair (GVR) architectures are a natural mitigation: stochastic generation produces candidates, deterministic verification finds violations, and repairs or human review close the loop [3].
sections.related_work: Three evidence strands motivate this study. First, empirical intent→config evaluations show LLMs can produce syntactically and semantically correct device commands in constrained settings, but those works do not systematically pair generator outputs with canonical verifiers and emulated execution traces to measure executed harm [1]. Second, multiple prototype and architectural studies propose multi‑agent and tool‑augmented stacks for NetOps that include verification components; these show design patterns but lack preregistered paired detection experiments against emulator outcomes [2]. Third, the generate–verify–repair literature from code and software engineering demonstrates that deterministic checks can improve end‑to‑end correctness when generator error prevalence is nontrivial, motivating similar end‑to‑end evaluation in NetOps while highlighting the importance of experimental contract choices (shared vs independent generation, repair allowance) [3]. Classical formal verification techniques (e.g., header‑space analysis, policy checkers) provide efficient reachability and policy invariants and are natural verifier candidates in GVR pipelines [4]. Our work situates a preregistered paired experimental test within these literatures and focuses on the narrowly defined estimand: verifier detection performance on identical generated candidates.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and estimand. We preregistered study c1-gnr-vv-2026-0001 and froze the confirmatory design, sampling plan, and analysis code prior to observing outcomes. The primary estimand is the paired reduction in undetected operational‑fault proportion (paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline). The confirmatory hypothesis H1 targeted an absolute paired reduction of 0.20 with two‑sided alpha = 0.05 and power ≥ 0.80; the preregistered N = 72 pairs stratified across three topology complexity strata (small/medium/complex).
sections.results: Execution and accounting. The registered execution completed without technical failures. Key deterministic counts from the execution manifest and reconciliation artifacts are: planned_episode_count = 144, completed_episode_count = 144, failed_episode_count = 0, model_calls_used = 72 (one shared initial generation per pair), and hosted_model_call_event_count = 72. The model configuration artifact (execution/model_configuration.json) declares requested_model = gpt-5-mini and temperature = null (provider default sampling semantics applied at runtime). The verifier used was deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator_version = "5.0").
sections.discussion: Confirmatory interpretation and ceiling effect. Under shared_initial_candidate semantics the identical generator output is evaluated in both baseline and guarded conditions. Observing zero baseline emulator faults yields a degenerate but informative outcome: there were no executed faults for the verifier to prevent, so the paired difference is necessarily zero. This result is not evidence that verifiers are unnecessary in all deployments; rather it reveals a limit of the chosen experimental contract for measuring verifier utility when baseline error prevalence is low.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered paired experiment to test whether a canonical deterministic verifier reduces the proportion of LLM-generated configurations that execute with operational faults. For the chosen model (gpt-5-mini), verifier (deterministic_netops_validator_v5), and task bank, baseline executions produced zero emulator faults and the verifier did not change outcomes (paired difference = 0.0, bootstrap 95% CI [0.0, 0.0], exact McNemar p = 1.0). Demonstrating verifier utility in practice will require experimental contracts that permit independent/multiple generations, repair‑enabled flows, adversarial tasks, and multi‑model comparisons. All execution artifacts and analysis logs referenced in this paper are archived in the evidence bundle to support replication and follow‑on studies.

limitations: Confirmatory ceiling/null outcome: baseline generator produced zero emulator faults on the preregistered task set, preventing direct measurement of verifier detection benefit.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics: the design measures verifier effect on the same generated candidate only and does not assess independent per‑condition generation, multi‑sample generation, or repairs unless explicitly permitted by the contract.
Single‑model scope: experiments used one declared model (gpt-5-mini); results do not imply generality across models or versions.
Synthetic/emulated tasks: task corpus and emulator executions differ from production devices and live traffic; external validity to production deployments is limited.

Sampling‑parameter uncertainty: execution/model_configuration.json shows temperature = null (sampling parameters unset); null indicates provider default sampling semantics determined runtime sampling behavior and is a recorded residual uncertainty.

Residual contamination risk: deterministic provenance and exact‑match checks were applied, but private training‑data contamination of the hosted model cannot be fully ruled out and remains residual uncertainty.
